title: Chip Butty
subtitle: Oven chips in soft white bread with ketchup or brown sauce
excerpt: Hot oven chips, heavily salted, put between thick slices of soft white bread with ketchup or brown sauce. One of the simplest and most satisfying British sandwiches.
sourceNotes: The chip butty is documented in British working-class food culture from the early twentieth century. It became widely popular after fried potato chips became available in fish-and-chip shops (from the 1860s onwards) and is now found across the country. Recipe developed from first principles.

content.text: A chip butty is hot chips in soft white bread. The bread must be soft enough to compress around the chips without resistance. The chips need to be properly hot and crisp so they do not steam the bread the moment they go in. Serve and eat without delay.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and cut into thick chips about 1 cm wide

content.text: Heat the oven to 220 degrees C. Peel {{potato}} of potato and cut into thick chips, roughly 1 cm wide. Toss on a baking tray with {{sunflower-oil}} of sunflower oil and a generous pinch of salt.
Spread in a single layer. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once halfway through, until golden and crisp at the edges. The thicker they are, the longer they need.
While the chips are still hot from the oven, butter {{bread-white}} slices if using. Shake malt vinegar over the chips if you like it.
Pile the chips onto the base slices. Add ketchup or brown sauce. Press the top slice down firmly enough that it grips the chips. Serve immediately.

rows.symptom: Chips are soft when they come out of the oven
rows.cause: Oven not hot enough, chips too close together, or moisture not driven off
rows.fix: Make sure the oven is properly preheated to 220 degrees C. Space the chips in a single layer with room between each one.

rows.cause: Chips too wet with oil or vinegar
rows.fix: Drain the chips briefly on a piece of kitchen paper if they are dripping. Go easy with the vinegar if you are using it.

rows.symptom: Chips fall out of the sandwich
rows.cause: Chips too thick or cut unevenly
rows.fix: Cut all the chips to a consistent thickness so they lie flat. Press the sandwich together firmly before cutting.
Season the chips before they go into the oven. They need salt from the start, not just at the end.

content.text: The chip butty is northern working-class food by origin, associated particularly with Yorkshire, Lancashire, and the Midlands, but eaten throughout Britain. It uses the cheapest possible ingredients and makes no apology for it. The combination of hot starch and soft bread is its point. Regional variations include the chip barm (in a bread roll rather than sliced bread), the chip cob, and the chip bap, all referring to the same idea with a different bread vessel.
